Issued at 1240 PM EST Thu Nov 12 2026


Pattern Synopsis/Forecast: Amplified upper-level pattern exists this 
afternoon across NOAM with overall little change to this anticipated 
through Friday night. Longwave troughing evident over the eastern 
half of continent, including the Great Lakes, with upstream ridging 
over the desert southwest northward through the Rockies. Sfc low 
pressure that passed through the Ohio Valley last night is now 
centered near MD/DE/NJ with cold air advection well underway locally 
in the wake of that system. Primary focus over the next ~48 hours 
will be on lake effect rain/snow potential, perhaps occasionally 
aided synoptically by mid-level perturbations pinwheeling through 
the aforementioned parent troughing overhead. 

Mid-upper level heights rise this weekend with upstream troughing 
making a run at the Great Lakes early next week. Some semblance of 
upper ridging (varying amplification) may continue through much of 
next week.  Largely dry conditions expected to return Sunday along 
with a return of above normal temperatures -- potentially through at 
least the middle to end of next week, as surface high pressure is 
expected to largely dominate the mid-upper MS Valley, Great Lakes, 
and Ohio Valley.

Forecast Details: Numerous showers ongoing early this afternoon, in 
particular across sections of northern lower MI. Some snow mixing in 
as well across higher terrain spots, even with a little bit of 
localized accumulation (Nubs Nob ski hill webcam showing a minor 
accum.). These showers aided by a mid-level wave currently departing 
to the south. By this evening, another incoming shortwave is 
expected to provide a renewed uptick in synoptic moisture/support, 
combined with an ample over-water thermal gradient (H8 temps -7 to -
10 C / delta Ts ranging from 18-21 C). Focus for this forecast 
package will largely be on the 18-hour window from this evening 
through midday Friday, especially near and west of Traverse City, 
given north to north-northeast low-level flow. Latest trends support 
a transition to mainly snow showers across parts of these areas this 
evening, especially away from the immediate lakeshores of Grand 
Traverse, Leelanau and Benzie counties. While the expectation is for 
lake effect banding to be fairly localized across these counties, 
heavier precip rates are likely to allow for a transition to all 
snow. Increasing moisture depth through the column and a deepening 
DGZ by late evening may support localized snowfall rates in excess 
of 1"/hr under heavier banding (especially as you increase elevation 
away from lake), and thus brings high probabilities for the season's 
first localized accumulation. Main limiting factor will be surface 
temps progged in the mid-30s, but this may become a moot point as 
evaporational cooling in any heavier banding sufficiently cools the 
surface temps several degrees. Ground temps are still warm and while 
this may have some effect on accumulation, past season's early 
events have proved that if it snows heavy enough, the ground temp 
really doesn't matter a whole lot. Highest probabilities (60-80%) 
for snow in excess of 2" by 18z Friday are highest across central 
Leelanau, north/northeast Benzie and western Grand Traverse. Lower 
probabilities (20-45%) of 4"+ across those same areas, and even some 
very localized non-zero (<10%) for accum greater than 8". All this 
said, favored accum. across these areas ranges from 1-4", with 
locally higher amounts possible. Will go ahead with a Winter Weather 
Advisory for Grand Traverse, Benzie and Leelanau counties -- again 
the highest accums favored for inland areas of western Grand 
Traverse, northern Benzie and central Leelanau.

Accumulation across northeast lower expected to be less tonight 
through midday Friday, but still may have some localized impacts. 
Probabilities away from the immediate lakeshores of Alcona/Iosco 
counties for 2"+ of snow range from 10-25% and ~5% chance for 4"+. 
Favored accumulation in these areas varied from 0.5 - 2.0", but 
it'll be a spot for monitoring for any potentially locally heavier 
banding. Elsewhere across northeast lower and across western 
Chip/Mack counties in the eastern U.P., generally an inch or less of 
snow is favored.

While some potential exists for the northwest lower advisory needing 
to be extended for part of the area beyond 18z Friday, confidence
decreases as winds begin shift more northerly Friday afternoon 
and eventually more north-northwesterly by late Friday night. 
Some accumulation potential exists through this time frame, 
especially in favored north flow lake effect areas, but continued
marginal surface temperatures, less favorable synoptic moisture
and shrinking inversion heights yields more uncertainty.
